title: Farid close
hook: a Sufi's humility near the end of the Guru's book: become the grass on the path

segments.voice: Yesterday, phika: Farid warned against the flat, harsh word, because every heart is a jewel. Your line was add one grain of sweetness.

Turn toward the last pages of the Guru Granth Sahib, among the short couplets, and a Muslim saint of the Punjab is still speaking there, signing his lines with his own name: Farid. This path has sat with him through a tree on a riverbank, a heart like a jewel, dry bread and cool water, a collar to look under before judging anyone. Today we close his pages with the thing under all the others: how low a person is willing to go.
screen: `A SUFI NEAR THE END OF THE BOOK.` → `A WEEK WITH FARID.` → `HOW LOW WILL YOU GO?`

segments.voice: One of Farid's couplets, from Ang 1378, in paraphrase: Farid, if you long for the Lord of all, become the grass on the path. One person cuts it, another tramples it. Then you'll be let into the Master's court. Grass by a footpath doesn't argue, or keep a list of who walked on it. It gets cut and grows back, low enough that nobody notices it, steady enough that the path stays green. Farid asks to be that. Now a careful second turn. Some readers worry this sounds like letting people walk all over you. But look at the Farid of these days. The same man told us to look under our own collar, and said that those with one thing in the heart and another on the lips are false. That isn't a doormat talking. His humility is sharp. It's the self that insists on being seen that he wants to lower, not the truth he's willing to say. The third turn is where these lines live: a Sufi of the Punjab, inside the book Sikhs bow to as their living Guru. Sikhs have a word for the quality Farid keeps returning to: nimrata, humility. Tradition says the Gurus treasured his verses, and the book keeps them near its close, in his own Punjabi, with his name in the lines. So his pages end not with a crown, but with grass, and a path, and a door that opens for the one who's willing to be low.
screen: `BECOME THE GRASS ON THE PATH.` · `CUT, TRAMPLED, GROWING BACK.` · `HUMBLE, BUT NOT SILENT.` · `HIS NAME IN THE LINES.` · then, large: `HUMBLE TO THE END.`

segments.voice: Choose one of Farid's lines from these days, the tree on the riverbank, every heart a jewel, dry bread and cool water, the collar, or the grass on the path, and say it slowly, once. Then sit with it, letting your breath go out longer than it comes in, the way grass bends; if one line keeps tugging at you, that's the one to keep. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Nimrata. Humility, the quality Farid's couplets keep returning to: not a crown, but grass that lets itself be cut and trampled, steady enough to keep the path green.
Your line: humble to the end. Low like grass, and still green. Farid's pages, closed.

howItsDone: Farid's couplets are read and sung in gurdwaras as gurbani alongside the Gurus' own hymns, and Sikhs often draw on them when speaking about nimrata, humility.

chat.says: Farid says be like grass that gets trampled. Isn't that letting people walk all over you?
options: No. He lowers the self that wants to be seen, not the truth he's willing to say.
Yes. Farid teaches that you should never speak up, even when something is wrong.
No. He meant it only for Sufi teachers, so their students would obey them.
chat.meaning: The same Farid who said look within your collar asks for nimrata: lower the self that insists on being seen, not the truth.

notes: Grass couplet ('Fareeda theeo pavaahee dabh, je saanee lorrhe sabh; ik chhijeh bia lataareeah, taa(n) saaee dai dar vaareeah') placed at Ang 1378: please confirm Ang and the paraphrase.
'Near the end' / 'last pages' describes the placement of the Salok Farid section near the close of the Granth; confirm the framing.
'Tradition says the Gurus treasured his verses' is attributed to tradition; no claim about how they were collected (see day 737).

Week look-back mentions days 763–766 (collar, dry bread, tree on the riverbank, every heart a jewel) and day 762 (heart and lips); y1 days 259–262 used the don't-strike-back, Creator-in-creation and crows couplets, so this day avoids them.
